newsitem.title: UK: New depository seen squeezing Indian GDR premiums.
newsitem.headline: New depository seen squeezing Indian GDR premiums.

text.p: Premiums of Indian global depositary receipts (GDR) to local market prices will contract as foreign investors increase local market dealings following the launch of a new depository system in India, Indosuez Asset Management Asia director Ayaz Ebrahim said.
"The central depository system will lead to a reduction in these premiums as foreign investors feel more comfortable being directly in India," he told the Reuters Market Forum conference.
The National Securities Depository started operating in December.
He said Indian GDRs had traded at an average premium to the local market of about 15 percent since January 1996.

He also said foreign investors who did deal directly in the local market should consider accessing the market through an offshore fund, rather than as an approved Foreign Institutional Investor (FII). He said the offshore funds offered certain advantages, such as no restrictions on the permitted size of a stake in a company and the ability to invest in the core money market.

FIIs cannot invest more than a total 24 percent in an Indian company, and an FII cannot take an individual stake of more than 10 percent. FIIs do not have access to the local money market, although restrictions on investment in government debt were lifted last week.
Already over 15 stocks have reached their foreign limits.
The funds also offered certain tax advantages, he said.
Another speaker said the Indian equity market was set for a strong 1997 despite relatively poor fundamentals.

Martin Currie Investment Management director Adrian Mowat said an expected sharp fall in interest rates in 1997, a weak gold price and a falling property market would see an upward equity market rerating, although concern remained about possible earnings downgrades.
